topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Add operations across stable element types without putting every report inside those classes. Worked example: Price a mixed workshop order. Each Part accepts a Visitor, and each concrete part forwards its own precise type. Price implements the type-specific operations and retains a checked running total.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Add a new operation without editing every existing part class.
Trace compile-time overload selection and runtime virtual dispatch.
Choose Visitor only when its type-set tradeoff fits the program.

blocks.text: Each element accepts a visitor through a shared interface. Its concrete accept implementation passes itself to the visitor entry point for that precise element type. The visitor supplies the operation for every supported type. Selection depends on both the actual element and actual visitor, a mechanism called double dispatch. Traversal decides which element comes next; acceptance decides which type-specific operation runs.

cards.question: What problem does Visitor address?
cards.answer: Add operations across stable element types without putting every report inside those classes. Worked example: Price a mixed workshop order. Each Part accepts a Visitor, and each concrete part forwards its own precise type. Price implements the type-specific operations and retains a checked running total.

cards.question: What is Visitor?
cards.answer: An operation object with a separate entry point for each supported element type.

cards.question: What is Overload resolution?
cards.answer: The compiler choosing a same-name function from its parameter types.

cards.question: What is Double dispatch?
cards.answer: Selecting behavior using both the actual element kind and actual operation kind.

cards.question: What is Closed type set?
cards.answer: A design that names all allowed element alternatives in one known interface or value type.

cards.question: Why can visitor.visit(part) not choose the Bolts overload from a Part reference?
cards.answer: C++ overload selection uses the expression’s static type. The concrete accept member supplies the precise Bolts type before the virtual visitor call.

cards.question: Why might ordinary virtual methods be better if new part types arrive every week?
cards.answer: Visitor requires a new type-specific entry and corresponding implementations across visitors. Ordinary virtual operations keep adding new types more local when the operation set stays stable.

cards.question: Why does visitor.visit(*this) choose a type-specific overload inside accept?
cards.answer: Inside Bolts::accept, *this has the Bolts type. Overload selection identifies visit(Bolts), then virtual dispatch chooses that operation's implementation on the actual visitor.

cards.question: What becomes expensive when adding a new Part kind?
cards.answer: Every Visitor implementation must support the new visit overload. Visitor favors adding operations over adding element types frequently.

cards.question: Why is adding Labels cheaper than editing every element's formatting method?
cards.answer: Labels adds a separate operation through the existing accept interface. Bolts and Cable need no new formatting-specific fields or methods.

cards.question: Can the same Price instance be reused for several parts?
cards.answer: Yes; it intentionally accumulates cents. Use a fresh visitor when a new independent total is required, or add an explicit reset contract.

cards.question: Why check the remaining price capacity before addition?
cards.answer: The one-million-cent limit is part of the visitor invariant. Rejection must leave the accumulated total unchanged instead of accepting a partial or wrapped value.

cards.question: Would a switch over a variant be a reasonable alternative?
cards.answer: Yes for a closed set of value-like element kinds. Both approaches make operations handle each kind; their maintenance costs differ in allocation, extensibility and compiler support.

cards.question: Why keep quantity validation in Bolts and Cable rather than Price?
cards.answer: Validity of an element must hold for every operation, including Labels. Putting it only in Price would let invalid elements reach other visitors.

topics.title: The problem: the parts stay familiar while reports multiply
topics.summary: A workshop order contains two kinds of item: a group of bolts counted by pieces, and a cable measured in whole metres. Each quantity must be between zero and one hundred. A price report charges five cents per bolt and forty cents per metre. The total cannot exceed one million cents. Direct price methods on Bolts and Cable are a reasonable first design when price is the one operation every item must offer. The next requests are labels, packing summaries, and audit reports, each with different output needs.

blocks.text: Adding every report as another virtual member makes stable data types change whenever a reporting team needs a new operation. A large switch on a type code moves the work outside the classes but loses compiler-checked access to the distinct data of each kind. We need to let an outside operation receive the exact kind of part while callers still traverse a mixed list through the common Part interface. The Visitor pattern provides this connection, at a cost: the set of element types becomes explicit in the visitor interface.

blocks.title: Excerpt - simplest starting point
blocks.code:
const int bolt_cost = bolts.count() * 5;
const int cable_cost = cable.metres() * 40;

discussion.answer: Each new operation forces changes to both element types. If the element kinds are stable but reports keep growing, separating operations can make extensions easier to review.

topics.title: One visitor operation has one entry point for each kind
topics.summary: Visitor declares two overloaded visit functions: one taking const Bolts& and one taking const Cable&. Overloading means several functions share a name but have different parameter lists. Price implements both. It keeps a running cents_ total and uses the correct unit for each kind. Bolts exposes a count getter; Cable exposes a metres getter. Neither class needs to know the price rules or the output format of a future label report.

blocks.text: Part declares accept(Visitor&) const. Each concrete element implements accept and calls visitor.visit with a reference to itself. The const qualifier at the end means this accepting operation cannot change the element through its ordinary members. The visitor reference is not const, because a report visitor may update its own running result. A read-only element and a changing report are compatible: const applies to a particular object and access path, not to the entire call tree.

topics.title: Why a single overloaded call is not enough
topics.summary: Imagine a Part& variable that actually refers to a Bolts object. Calling visitor.visit(part) cannot select visit(const Bolts&) merely because the runtime object happens to be bolts. Overload resolution, the choice among same-name functions, uses the expression’s static type during compilation. Here the static type is Part&, and Visitor does not offer a Part overload. A downcast at every caller would move type-checking knowledge into all loops, defeating the goal of a common traversal.

blocks.text: Instead the loop calls part->accept(price). Virtual dispatch chooses Bolts::accept during execution because the actual element is Bolts. Inside that member, *this has the type const Bolts, so the compiler selects visit(const Bolts&) when compiling that function. Calling the selected virtual visit then dispatches to the implementation belonging to the actual visitor object, Price. The behavior depends on both the element kind and visitor kind. This two-stage selection is called double dispatch. It combines static overload choice with virtual calls; it does not make ordinary C++ overload resolution dynamic.

topics.title: Follow ownership without giving it to the visitor
topics.summary: The parts vector owns unique_ptr<Part> values whose actual objects are Bolts and Cable. Part has a virtual destructor so destroying an owning base pointer properly destroys the complete concrete object. Price is a separate local object in main. During accept it borrows each part through a const reference. It does not retain those references, own the parts, or change their quantities. After traversal, the visitor owns only its numeric result.

blocks.text: The forward declarations class Bolts and class Cable tell the compiler that those type names exist before Visitor uses references to them. A reference declaration does not need the complete class layout. The later class definitions provide constructors, getters, and accept bodies. This arrangement resolves the header dependency between the visitor interface and its element types. In a multi-file program, separate headers and forward declarations keep that dependency controlled; putting every implementation in one header can make every report change trigger broad recompilation.

topics.title: The price calculation also needs ordinary correctness
topics.summary: Design structure does not make arithmetic automatically safe. Constructors reject negative quantities and quantities above one hundred. Each price term is therefore bounded before multiplication: at most five hundred cents for bolts or four thousand cents for cable. Price::add checks whether the accumulated total exceeds one million minus the next nonnegative term. Only then does it add. Checking before addition avoids computing an overflowed result and trying to diagnose it afterward. The chosen limits fit the required int range on the documented compiler platform.

blocks.text: The sample order contains three bolts and two metres of cable. The terms are fifteen and eighty, so the result is ninety-five cents. A fresh visitor starts at zero; a zero-quantity element changes nothing. For the limit test, two hundred fifty visits to a one-hundred-metre cable reach exactly one million. The next visit throws and leaves the old total intact. The visitor therefore has its own invariant and failure policy, separate from those of the elements. Reusing the same Price visitor for another order would accumulate into the previous result unless the caller deliberately creates a new visitor.

topics.title: Choose which direction of change should be easy
topics.summary: Adding Labels in the lab changes no Bolts, Cable, or Part class. Labels implements both visits and appends strings with quantities and unit names. The same traversal works. However, adding a new element kind such as Paint requires a new visit overload in the Visitor interface and an implementation in every concrete visitor. This can be useful: the compiler forces every operation to decide how to handle Paint. It can also be costly when new element kinds arrive frequently and the operation set barely changes.

blocks.text: C++17 offers another option for a closed set of types: std::variant<BoltsData, CableData> can store exactly one alternative, and std::visit selects a callable for the active alternative. This can avoid a heap allocation and a virtual base hierarchy for simple value data. It still makes the type set explicit, and visitors must handle its alternatives. Ordinary virtual members remain simpler when new types are common and the operation set is stable. Visitor is a tradeoff between these directions of change, not a general rule to move every method out of its class.

topics.title: Exercise 22.6: Justify a decision
topics.summary: Explain when std::variant and std::visit would be preferable to this hierarchy. Include a cost of the choice.

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: Consider simple value data and a closed list of alternatives.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: A variant fits a small closed set of value records and can store them without separate heap objects. Its type list appears in the value type, so adding an alternative can affect many callers and visitors. A polymorphic hierarchy can be more flexible when elements have independent identity and richer lifetimes.

workshop.title: Price a mixed workshop order
workshop.problem: Price a mixed workshop order. Support bolt counts and cable lengths with distinct units. Compute exact integer-cent totals with a one-million-cent limit. Keep reporting operations outside stable part data classes.

steps.state: parts[0] owns Bolts(3), traversed through Part.
steps.why: The pointer static type hides which concrete element it owns.
The actual element type controls the first dispatch.

steps.state: Inside accept, self is const Bolts&.
steps.why: Compile-time overload resolution selects the Bolts visit signature.
The actual visitor type controls the second dispatch.
Its accept selects the Cable overload with metres as the unit.

workshop.pitfall: Call visit directly with a Part reference and expect the Bolts overload to be chosen dynamically. The call does not compile with this interface because neither concrete-reference overload accepts a Part reference. Overload resolution uses the static expression type; accept supplies the missing concrete-type step.

discussion.question: New reports arrive weekly, while the two element kinds have stayed fixed for years. Choose Visitor or adding every report as a new Part virtual member.
discussion.answer: Visitor is a reasonable fit: each report implements the known type cases without editing every element. It introduces a shared type list, so document that adding a new part kind affects all report visitors.

workshop.alternative: Virtual price members are simpler if price is intrinsic and the operation set is stable. A variant and std::visit suit a closed set of simple value types. Visitor is useful when adding operations across stable element types is the main change.
workshop.design: Each Part accepts a Visitor, and each concrete part forwards its own precise type. Price implements the type-specific operations and retains a checked running total.
invariants: Each part quantity is in 0 through 100.
Price is between zero and one million cents.
A visitor reads parts without taking ownership.
Every concrete visitor supplies an operation for every declared element kind.
workshop.maintenance: A new report becomes a visitor with an explicit case for every type. A new type becomes a deliberate cross-operation change; use compiler errors and tests to locate all affected report behavior.
workshop.verification: The executable checks a mixed order total, a fresh empty result, zero quantity, rejected negative cable length, exact price limit, and rejection above the limit without mutation. The code guards upper quantity bounds, but the primary tests do not enumerate every constructor bound.
